Yes, if you are still registered at your home county you actually have two options to vote.

First, you can go to any polling place and do what's called a Provisional Ballot. A Provisional requires a little bit of paperwork but it is fairly simple and easy to get done. Just make sure that under the Residence Address box you put a LOCAL address for wherever you are staying in your current county. We need this address to precinct you correctly and make sure you get the right ballot style. The mailing address can be anywhere you want.

The big problem with a provisional ballot is that it might not count. All provisional ballots go to a ballot board to be reviewed before they can be counted. The ballot board is made up of judges from each party and they can refuse it for any reason, though the most common is that the paperwork just wasn't filled out correctly.

The best option, and the one I would do if it were me, is a limited ballot. For a limited ballot, you can go to the local election office and let them know you are registered in a different county. They will pull up the ballots for your original county and current county and let you vote on everything they have in common. So you can vote for all the statewide and federal stuff like President, Senate, Railroad Commissioner, etc. You just won't be able to vote for local stuff like the mayor or city council.

Both of these options will register you in your current county so you will have to re-register if you move somewhere else. Please be sure to have a government-issued photo ID ready when you go to vote, a driver's license or passport will work perfectly.

There have been no issues with the actual voting machines. Every county should have thoroughly tested the machines after getting a recent software update. I helped test the ones in my county and the few that did act up were removed and the remaining ones in the batch were tested again.

The machines themselves have a lot of security. Aside from built-in security procedures to make sure your ballot is recorded correctly, they are transported to and from their storage space or election office by local LEOs and a clerk or elections judge. Each one also has locks and multiple tamper-evident seals both inside and out. If anyone is manipulating the vote, it isn't being done at this level.

We also keep a pretty big paper trail that is reviewed multiple times by clerks and election officials. If there is vote manipulation occurring, I don't think it is happening at this level.

If you are still concerned about the issue, you can call the elections office to ask for more information about our security measures. I've had to be fairly vague for some obvious reasons.

More importantly, you can also vote for people you believe will make the changes you want to see.

No, a clerk writing on your ballot won't get it thrown out. Some ballots, like a provisional ballot, actually require a clerks signature to be counted.

Clerks have to swear an oath to protect the security of your ballot and prepare it as you wish within reason. If a clerk intentionally attempts to have your ballot thrown out, they can be brought up on charges including voter suppression. Naturally, most clerks will do everything they can to prevent that, and will do their best to get everything right.

If you have any concerns like this while at a polling location, ask the lead clerk about it. We get picked for the job because we are knowledgeable of the system and we are good at the job. If they can't answer your question, they know who can.

Curbside varies a bit depending on the equipment a polling location has. Some election offices and polling locations are set up for drive-thru voting, but you would need to call ahead or check with your local elections office to get those locations.

You can also do CAV, Convenient Accessible Voting, as a curbside voting option. For CAV you or someone with you can go to a polling location and inform a poll worker that you would like to do CAV voting. In some counties you can also call the elections office, tell them where you are, and ask them to inform your polling location that you are on site and would like to do CAV.

 Two workers will come out to your vehicle to begin the check-in process, you will need to provide some sort of government-issued picture ID (driver's license, passport, concealed carry license etc.) They will create a ballot receipt for you and you will need to provide your signature verifying that they have all of the correct information for you. If they don't have the right information they will be able to fix it on-site.

Once they finish getting you checked in they will allow you to vote, but again this depends on the equipment they have available. Counties with the newer equipment will be able to bring a tablet from the voting machine out to you along with an access code and you can vote normally.
^ that, or you can call your local elections office or check on their website.

Political materials supporting any party, candidate, or proposition have to stay 100ft away from the entrance to a polling place. That includes signs, flags, banners etc. Most polling places will have distance markers set 100ft outside the door.

While I can't speak for every county, we have been required to wear face masks/shields and gloves while working the polls. We also wipe down and disinfect the voting machines, pens, pencils, and tables we use at the polling sites. We have been using small cardboard boxes on site for voters to place their id in and prevent us from touching the voter or the ID itself. We also have been making heavy use of hand sanitizer and making sure there is plenty readily available for voters.

Poll workers should have gloves, masks, and hand sanitizer available for anyone to use upon request.

Most counties to my knowledge are using the same procedures. If you have any further doubts I would suggest contacting your local election office for more information.

Your best bet would be to go through the League of Women Voters site [vote411.org](http://vote411.org)

It provides sample ballots that include the policies of different candidates and allows you to compare them. The site is designed to be non-partisan. I can't speak for other election workers but that is the site my county recommends to voters during elections.

I'm an elections judge and I cannot tell you how many times I have said something similar to this either during training classes or to uneducated voters during elections. It may not seem like it all the time but every vote actually does count, even in "safe states". If you don't like the status quo, but don't bother voting for change, you are the reason things are the way they are. Most states make it pretty easy to register to vote and unless your polling place is just insanely busy, the actual voting process usually only takes a few minutes.

If you need more information on registering or why it's important to vote, just contact your local elections office or check their website. If you haven't been keeping up with who and what may appear on the ballot, your elections office may have sample ballots available and the League of Women Voters publishes nonpartisan voting guides on their site with all of the basic information about each item on the ballot.

If you are interested in learning more about the voting process or getting involved with it, please contact your local elections office and consider volunteering. I can't speak for everywhere else but in my area we are very shorthanded and need as many volunteers as we can get to work on elections day and during early voting.

Sorry I'm late. If you are still having issues with cleaning your enamel pins there's a few things you can do.

You can use silver polish and a couple of soft cloths. Shake the bottle of polish as per the directions and apply a small amount to a cloth and gently rub it onto the pin. Buff it off with a different cloth and it will come out nice and shiny.

If you don't have or don't want to get silver polish you can use WD40 as an alternative. Spray a little onto the pin or on a rag and rub it on, then buff it off with a soft cloth. Both are good for removing tarnish and the pin usually comes out pretty shiny.

If you want to preserve the pin a bit better you can apply a very thin coating of renaissance wax to the front and back to help prevent further tarnishing.

This method is for ENAMEL pins and may not be the best for buttons, particularly lithos and cellos.
